title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (film)
wiki_lead:
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest is a 1975 American psychological comedy-drama film directed by Miloš Forman, based on the 1962 novel of the same name by Ken Kesey. The film stars Jack Nicholson as a new patient at a mental institution and Louise Fletcher as the abusive head nurse. Will Sampson, Danny DeVito, Sydney Lassick, William Redfield, Christopher Lloyd, and Brad Dourif play supporting roles, with the latter two making their feature-film debuts and Sampson having never acted before.
Originally announced in 1962 with Kirk Douglas starring, the film took 13 years to develop. Filming finally began in January 1975 and lasted three months, on location in Salem, Oregon, and the surrounding area, and in Depoe Bay on the north Oregon coast. The producers shot the film in the Oregon State Hospital, an actual psychiatric hospital, which is also the novel's setting. The hospital is still in operation, though the original buildings in the film have been demolished. The film was released on November 19, 1975.
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest received critical acclaim and is considered by critics and audiences to be one of the greatest films ever made. It is the second of three films to win all five major Academy Awards (Best Picture, Best Actor, Best Actress, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay) following It Happened One Night (1934) and preceding 1991's The Silence of the Lambs. It won numerous Golden Globe and BAFTA Awards. In 1993, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the United States Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry. Additionally, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest was ranked number 33 on the American Film Institute's updated 100 Years... 100 Movies list in 2007.

Plot
In 1963 Oregon, Randle McMurphy is incarcerated for his statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl and five previous arrests for assault. He feigns mental illness so he can be moved to a mental institution and avoid hard labor at a work farm. The medical ward is dominated by the cold, passive-aggressive Nurse Ratched, who maintains control over the patients through intimidation. Among them are young, anxious, stuttering Billy Bibbit; Charlie Cheswick, who is prone to temper tantrums; delusional, child-like Martini; the articulate and repressed homosexual Dale Harding; belligerent and profane Max Taber; epileptics Jim Sefelt and Bruce Fredrickson; quiet but violent-minded Scanlon; tall, huge, and deaf-mute Euro-Indigenous American Chief Bromden; and several others with chronic conditions.
Ratched sees McMurphy's lively, rebellious presence as a threat to her authority, and she rations the patients' cigarettes and suspends their card-playing privileges. McMurphy bets the other inmates he can escape by hurling a hydrotherapy fountain through a locked window, but unsurprisingly is unable to lift the heavy device. grok_lead: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest is a 1975 American drama film directed by MiloÅ¡ Forman, adapted from Ken Kesey's 1962 novel of the same name. The story centers on Randle Patrick McMurphy, a recidivist criminal played by Jack Nicholson, who manipulates a psychiatric evaluation to escape prison labor and enters a state mental hospital, where he confronts the rigid control exerted by head nurse Mildred Ratched, portrayed by Louise Fletcher. Produced on a modest budget of approximately $4.4 million, the film explores themes of individual liberty versus institutional conformity through McMurphy's disruptive influence on the patients and staff. Released on November 19, 1975, by United Artists, the film achieved both critical acclaim and commercial triumph, grossing over $163 million worldwide and becoming one of the highest-grossing films of its era relative to cost. At the 48th Academy Awards, it swept the five major categoriesâBest Picture, Best Director, Best Actor, Best Actress, and Best Adapted Screenplayâmarking the first such achievement since It Happened One Night in 1934. These wins underscored the film's portrayal of authoritarian overreach in psychiatric institutions, drawing from real mid-20th-century practices like lobotomies and electroconvulsive therapy, though Kesey himself criticized the adaptation for shifting narrative focus from the Native American patient Chief Bromden to McMurphy and omitting key psychedelic elements from the source material. The film's enduring legacy stems from its stark depiction of power dynamics, influencing discussions on mental health treatment and personal autonomy without romanticizing mental illness or endorsing unchecked rebellion; its success derived from Forman's use of mostly non-professional actors from Oregon's mental institutions for authenticity, enhancing realism over sensationalism. Despite Kesey's legal disputes over rights and creative controlâwhich he lost due to prior sale of adaptation optionsâthe movie's independent merits propelled it to status as a cinematic milestone, ranked among the greatest films for its unflinching critique of bureaucratic oppression.
